readerTitle: The pan that won every test and still sat in the warehouse
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방용품 도매업체, 사내 데이터팀) · 모든 상황은 설명용
insight: 메시지는 제품을 설명하는 글이 아니라, 듣는 사람이 이미 느끼는 문제와 제품을 잇는 다리다. 같은 제품도 듣는 시장이 바뀌면 메시지가 바뀌어야 한다.
misconception: 제품이 좋고 설명이 정확하면 메시지는 저절로 통한다. 장점을 더 많이, 더 자세히 말할수록 설득력이 커진다.

sources.text: 마케팅 실무의 일반 개념 (메시지-시장 적합성, 고객 언어로 말하기)
모든 사례와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. 실제 기업, 연구, 통계를 인용하지 않았는지 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요.
'message-market fit'은 업계에서 쓰이는 표현이며 특정 인물의 상표나 프레임워크로 소개하지 않았습니다. 용어 기원을 특정인에게 귀속하지 않도록 유지하세요.

cards.title: The pan that won every test and still sat in the warehouse
body: A kitchenware wholesaler launches a new frying pan. Home cooks in testing love it. The sales sheet is proud and precise: *patented five-layer ceramic coating, heat-tested to extreme temperatures.*
The sales team calls on two hundred independent kitchen shops. Almost none place an order. The pan is good. The pitch is accurate. Something else is wrong.

image.label: Stacked boxes of frying pans in a quiet warehouse
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고 선반에 같은 프라이팬 상자가 높이 쌓여 있고 먼지가 살짝 앉은 느낌. 상자 옆면에 "5-layer ceramic" 같은 작은 기술 문구. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Why won't the shops stock it?
body: The price to shops matches rival pans. Samples were offered. Buyers listened politely, then said "maybe next season."

options.text: The price is still too high for small shops
options.feedback: Price always matters, but it matched rivals. Cutting it would shrink the margin without answering what buyers actually weigh.

options.text: The pitch describes what the maker is proud of, not what a shop owner worries about
options.feedback: A shop buyer isn't cooking with the pan. They're asking whether it sells, whether it comes back, and what they keep. The pitch answered none of that.

options.text: Not enough people know the brand yet, so it needs more advertising
options.feedback: More ads spread the same message further. If the message misses, you pay more to miss more people.

cards.title: Same pan. New words.
body: The sales lead asks five shop owners what makes a pan a bad stock choice. The answers repeat: *customers bring it back when the coating peels*, and *it sits on the shelf because nobody can tell it apart.*
The new pitch leads with those worries: a coating built to stop peeling returns, a display box that shows eggs sliding off, and the shop's margin per pan.
Nothing about the product changed. Orders start coming in.

cards.title: Message-market fit
body: **Message-market fit** means your words match what a specific group of customers already cares about, in language they already use.
It has two halves. The *market*: who exactly is listening. The *message*: the problem you name and the promise you make. A message can be true, clever and well designed and still fit nobody.

image.label: Two puzzle pieces: listener's worry and the message
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 퍼즐 조각 "What they already worry about", 오른쪽 조각 "What you say". 위쪽 그림은 조각이 어긋나 있고("Coating specs" vs "Returns, shelf, margin"), 아래 그림은 딱 맞물림.

cards.title: Three tests a message has to pass.
body: Before a message goes out, check it from the listener's chair.
list: **Their problem:** it names something they already feel, not something you must convince them of
**Their words:** it uses the phrases they use, not your internal or technical terms
**Their proof:** it offers evidence they trust, such as a demo, a peer, or a number they track
cards.callout: Listen for the words customers repeat. Those are your message.

cards.title: One product can need several messages.
body: The wholesaler now has two audiences. Shop owners hear about returns and margin. Home cooks in the shop see *"Eggs slide off, even without oil."*
Neither message is more true. Each fits a different listener. The mistake is picking one message and pointing it at everyone.

image.label: One pan, two speech bubbles for two audiences
image.brief: 가운데 프라이팬 하나. 왼쪽 가게 주인 캐릭터 옆 말풍선 "Fewer returns", 오른쪽 요리하는 손님 옆 말풍선 "Eggs slide off". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: A security tool might tell IT teams "fewer alerts to chase" and tell finance "one bill instead of four vendors." Same product, different buyers, different first sentence.

cards.title: A message can't fix a product that misses.
body: If the pan really did peel, a sharper pitch would only speed up the returns. Message-market fit helps a good product get heard. It doesn't replace one.
Judge a message by what people do, such as orders, replies and sign-ups, not by compliments. And don't rewrite it weekly. Change one thing, then watch long enough to see a difference.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: Your internal data team built a dashboard for regional sales managers. Few have opened it. The managers spend Friday mornings guessing which deals will close before the forecast call.
Which message should lead the next announcement?

options.text: "Every sales metric in one place, updated live"
options.feedback: Accurate and tidy, but it describes the tool. It doesn't name the Friday problem managers already feel.

options.text: "See which deals are likely to slip before Friday's forecast call"
options.feedback: It names their pain in their words and ties to a moment they dread. You give up the full feature list to win the first click.

options.text: "Built on the company's new data platform and approved by IT"
options.feedback: That reassures IT, not sales managers. It answers a question this audience isn't asking.

cards.title: Say what they already worry about, in their words.
body: A good product with the wrong message looks like a bad product. Fit the message to one listener before you make it louder.
**Try it today:** ask three customers what almost stopped them from buying. Compare their exact words with the first line of your pitch.
